The travel nut continues to move slightly beyond the limit of jaw travel, just enough to relieve some of the spring pressure on the conical clutch surfaces. As long as the starter continues to rotate, there is just enough pressure on the conical clutch surfaces to provide torque on the spiral splines that balance most of the pressure of the jaw spring. If the engine fails to start, the starter jaw does not retract since the starter mechanism provides no retracting force. However, when the engine fires and the engine jaw overruns the starter jaw, the sloping ramps of the jaw teeth force the starter jaw into the starter against the jaw spring pressure. This disengages the conical clutch surfaces entirely, and the jaw spring pressure forces the traveling nut to slide in along the spiral splines until the conical clutch surfaces are again in contact. When the starter and engine are both running, there is an engaging force keeping the jaws in contact that continue until the starter is de-energized. However, the rapidly moving engine jaw teeth, striking the slowly moving starter jaw teeth, hold the starter jaw disengaged. As soon as the starter comes to rest, the engaging force is removed, and the small return spring throws the starter jaw into its fully retracted position where it remains until the next start. When the starter jaw first engages the engine jaw, the motor armature has had time to reach considerable speed because of its high starting torque. The sudden engagement of the moving starter jaw with the stationary engine jaw would develop forces sufficiently high enough to severely damage the engine or the starter were it not for the plates in the clutch pack that slip when the engine torque exceeds the clutch-slipping torque. In normal direct cranking action, the internal steel gear clutch plates are held stationary by the friction of the bronze plates with which they are interleaved. When the engine reaches the speed that the starter is trying to achieve, the torque drops off to a value less than the clutch setting, the internal gear clutch plates are again held stationary, and the jaw rotates at the speed that the motor is attempting to drive it. summary.long_summary:
The engine start sequence requires the engine selector switch to be set, and the starter and safety switches—wired in series—to be closed before the starter can be energized. Power to the starter control circuit is supplied through a circuit breaker labeled “Starter, Primer, and Induction Vibrator.” When the selector is in the start position, closing the starter switch energizes a starter relay in the nacelle, completing the power path to the starter motor via the master bus and starter bus cable.

All starters have time limits to prevent overheating. After a 1‑minute cranking period the starter must cool for at least 1 minute; after any subsequent 1‑minute cranking, a 5‑minute cooling period is required.

**Manual direct‑cranking systems** use an overrunning clutch and a pinion that engages the crankshaft gear. A cockpit knob or handle pulls a flexible control rod, moving a lever that shifts the pinion into mesh and closes the starter switch. A return spring returns the lever to the off position. Proper pinion travel is critical before the adjustable stud contacts the switch.

**Automatic (remote‑solenoid) systems** activate a starter solenoid via a push‑button or ignition key. The solenoid closes its contacts, energizing the starter motor. The motor’s initial rotation engages an overrunning clutch in a starter adapter that contains worm‑reduction gears.

**Right‑angle drive adapters** employ a worm shaft and gear that engage a starter shaft gear through a spring‑clutch assembly. When the engine fires, the clutch spring disengages, allowing the shaft gear to rotate the crankshaft directly.

**Ring‑gear starters** mount a drive gear on the propeller hub. The electric motor spins the gear, which moves outward to mesh with the ring gear, cranking the engine. As the engine reaches self‑sustaining speed, the drive gear is driven back and disengages.

**Maintenance practices** for these systems include replacing starter motor brushes and brush springs, cleaning dirty commutators, and machining (turning down) any burned or out‑of‑round components to ensure reliable operation.

Chapter 5

Engine Starting Systems

Introduction

Most aircraft engines, reciprocating or turbine, require help during the starting process. Hence, this device is termed the starter. A starter is an electromechanical mechanism capable of developing large amounts of mechanical energy that can be applied to an engine, causing it to rotate. Reciprocating engines need only to be turned through at a relatively slow speed until the engine starts and turns on its own. Once the reciprocating engine has fired and started, the starter is disengaged and has no further function until the next start. In the case of a turbine engine, the starter must turn the engine up to a speed that provides enough airflow through the engine for fuel to be ignited. Then, the starter must continue to help the engine accelerate to a self-sustaining speed. Turbine engine starters have a critical role in starting of the engine.

If the starter turns the turbine engine up to a self-sustaining speed, the engine start process will be successful. There are only a few types or methods used to turn the engine. Almost all reciprocating engines use a form of electric motor geared to the engine. Modern turbine engines use electric motors, starter/generators (electric motor and a generator in the same housing), and air turbine starters. Air turbine starters are driven by compressed air through a turbine wheel that is mechanically connected through reduction gears to one of the engine's compressors, generally the highest pressure compressor.

Reciprocating Engine Starting Systems

In the early stages of aircraft development, relatively low powered reciprocating engines were started by pulling the propeller through a part of a revolution by hand. Difficulty was often experienced in cold weather starting when lubricating oil temperatures were near the congealing point. In addition, the magneto systems delivered a weak starting spark at the very low cranking speeds. This was often compensated for by providing a hot spark using such ignition system devices as the booster coil, induction vibrator, or impulse coupling.

Some small, low-powered aircraft which use hand-cranking of the propeller, or propping, for starting are still being operated. For general instructions on starting this type of aircraft, refer to the Aviation Maintenance Technician—General Handbook, Chapter 1, Safety, Ground Operations, and Servicing. Throughout the development of the aircraft reciprocating engine from the earliest use of starting systems to the present, a number of different starter systems have been used. Most reciprocating engine starters are the direct cranking electric type. A few older model aircraft are still equipped with inertia starters. Thus, only a brief description of these starting systems is included in this section.

Inertia Starters

There are three general types of inertia starters: hand, electric, and combination hand and electric. The operation of all types of inertia starters depends on the kinetic energy stored in a rapidly rotating flywheel for cranking ability. Kinetic energy is energy possessed by a body by virtue of its state of motion, which may be movement along a line or spinning action.

summary.title: Engine Starting Systems: Types and Inertia Starter Overview
summary.long_summary: Chapter 5 introduces aircraft engine starters, devices that supply the mechanical energy needed to rotate an engine until it can run on its own. Reciprocating engines require only a slow turn to reach ignition, after which the starter disengages. Turbine engines need the starter to accelerate the compressor to a speed that provides sufficient airflow for fuel ignition and then continue to aid until a self‑sustaining speed is reached. The chapter outlines the few common starter types: electric motors (often geared), starter‑generators that combine motor and generator functions, and air turbine starters powered by compressed air driving a turbine linked through reduction gears to a compressor. Historically, low‑power reciprocating engines were hand‑propelled, a method still used on some small aircraft, but cold‑weather conditions and weak magneto sparks made this difficult, leading to auxiliary ignition devices such as booster coils and impulse couplings. The text then describes inertia starters, which store kinetic energy in a rapidly rotating flywheel. Three variants exist—hand‑operated, electric, and combined hand‑electric—each releasing the stored energy through a clutch system to crank the engine. faqs.question: Why does the air turbine starter not operate (no rotation)?
faqs.answer: Possible causes are no air supply, an open circuit in the cutoff switch, a sheared starter drive coupling, or an internal starter discrepancy. Check the air supply, verify switch continuity and replace the switch if needed, replace the drive coupling, or replace the starter.

faqs.question: What should I do if the starter will not accelerate to normal cutoff speed?
faqs.answer: Check the air source pressure, adjust the rotor switch actuator, replace the pressure‑regulating valve if it is set too low, or replace the starter if there is an internal malfunction.

faqs.question: Why won't the starter cut off at the proper speed?
faqs.answer: Low air supply, a rotor switch actuator set too high, or a shorted starter cutoff switch can prevent cut‑off. Verify the air supply, adjust the switch actuator assembly, and replace the switch and bracket assembly if necessary.

faqs.question: What causes external oil leakage from the starter?
faqs.answer: External oil leaks can be caused by oil level that is too high, loose vent, oil filler, or magnetic plugs, or a loose clamp‑band assembly. Drain the oil and service it properly, tighten the magnetic plug to the proper torque, and secure the vent, filler plugs and clamp band as specified.

faqs.question: The starter runs but the engine does not turn over. What is the likely problem?
faqs.answer: A sheared drive coupling is the usual cause. Remove the starter and replace the drive coupling; if couplings repeatedly break, replace the starter.

faqs.question: Why won't the starter inlet line up with the supply ducting?
faqs.answer: Improper installation of the starter on the engine or incorrect indexing of the turbine housing can cause misalignment. Verify installation and indexing against the manufacturer’s instructions and the required turbine housing index position for the aircraft.

faqs.question: What do metallic particles on the magnetic drain plug indicate?
faqs.answer: Fuzzy, small particles are normal wear. Coarser particles such as chips or slivers indicate internal difficulty; in that case, replace the starter.

faqs.question: What should be done if broken nozzle vanes are found?
faqs.answer: Broken vanes are caused by large foreign particles in the air supply. Replace the starter and inspect the air‑supply filter for contamination.

faqs.question: How can I resolve oil leakage from the vent plug assembly?
faqs.answer: Oil leakage from the vent plug assembly is usually due to improper starter installation position. Check the installed position for proper levelness of the oil plugs and correct it according to the manufacturer’s installation instructions.

faqs.question: What is the remedy for oil leakage at the drive coupling?
faqs.answer: Oil leakage at the drive coupling is caused by a leaking rear seal assembly. Remove and replace the starter.

summary.title: Air Turbine Starter Operation and Troubleshooting
summary.long_summary:
The air turbine starter uses pressurized air to spin a turbine, which drives a gear train and an overrunning clutch to rotate the engine’s output shaft. As the turbine accelerates, the inboard clutch gear, threaded onto a helical screw, moves forward and its teeth engage the outboard clutch gear, delivering power to the engine. When the starter reaches cut‑out speed, the start valve closes; after air flow stops, the outboard gear, now driven by the engine, overtakes the inboard gear, causing the clutch to disengage and allowing the rotor to coast down while the outboard shaft continues to turn with the engine.

A troubleshooting guide (Figure 5‑25) lists common problems, probable causes, and recommended remedies for air turbine starters equipped with a combined pressure‑regulating and shut‑off valve. Issues covered include:
• No starter rotation – check air supply, cutoff‑switch continuity, drive coupling, or replace the starter.
• Failure to reach normal cut‑off speed – verify air pressure, switch actuator setting, valve pressure, or replace the starter.
• Starter does not cut off – inspect air supply, adjust switch actuator, replace switch/bracket.
• External oil leaks – drain excess oil, tighten vent, filler, magnetic plugs, or clamp band.
• Engine does not turn over despite starter running – replace sheared drive coupling.
• Misalignment of starter inlet – confirm proper installation and turbine housing indexing.
• Metallic particles on drain plug – normal wear if fuzzy; replace starter if coarse chips appear.
• Broken nozzle vanes – caused by foreign particles; replace starter and check air filter.
• Oil leakage from vent plug or drive coupling – correct installation position or replace rear seal assembly.
The guide emphasizes using these steps as a reference while always following the manufacturer’s specific instructions.

summary.title: Electric Inertia and Direct Cranking Starter Systems Overview
summary.long_summary:
The passage describes two primary types of engine starting systems used on reciprocating engines. First, the electric inertia starter is illustrated in Figures 5‑1 to 5‑3. It consists of a small motor, a flywheel, movable gears, a meshing solenoid, and a torque‑overload release clutch. When the starter is energized, the motor drives the flywheel and all internal components. After full energization, a cable or an electrically actuated meshing solenoid engages the flywheel to the engine crankshaft, transferring stored kinetic energy through reduction gears and the overload clutch to start the engine. Figure 5‑2 shows the associated electrical circuit, which includes a battery, relay, control switches, a starter solenoid, and mesh points tied to the bus and ground.

The second system, the direct‑cranking electric starter, is the most common across all engine types. It provides immediate, continuous cranking as soon as it is powered. Its main elements are an electric motor, reduction gears, and an automatic engage/disengage mechanism operated by an adjustable torque‑overload release clutch. Figure 5‑4 presents a typical circuit for this starter, featuring heavy‑duty cables from the starter to the battery capable of carrying currents up to about 350 A, a battery solenoid, a battery switch, a starter solenoid, and a remote starter switch. The use of solenoids and remote switching reduces cable weight and minimizes voltage drop in the circuit.

Overall, the text outlines the mechanical components, operational sequence, and electrical schematics of both inertia‑type and direct‑cranking starters, emphasizing the role of solenoids, heavy‑current wiring, and overload clutches in reliable engine start‑up.

Gas Turbine Engine Starters

Gas turbine engines are started by rotating the high-pressure compressor. On dual-spool, axial flow engines, the high-pressure compressor and N1 turbine system is only rotated by the starter. To start a gas turbine engine, it is necessary to accelerate the compressor to provide sufficient air to support combustion in the combustion section, or burners. Once ignition and fuel have been introduced and the lite-off has occurred, the starter must continue to assist the engine until the engine reaches a self-sustaining speed. The torque supplied by the starter must be in excess of the torque required to overcome compressor inertia and the friction loads of the engine's compressor.

Figure 5-14 illustrates a typical starting sequence for a gas turbine engine, regardless of the type of starter employed. As soon as the starter has accelerated the compressor sufficiently to establish airflow through the engine, the ignition is turned on followed by the fuel. The exact sequence of the starting procedure is important since there must be sufficient airflow through the engine to support combustion before the air-fuel mixture is ignited. At low engine cranking speeds, the fuel flow rate is not sufficient to enable the engine to accelerate; for this reason, the starter continues to crank the engine until after self-accelerating speed has been attained. If assistance from the starter were cut off below the self-accelerating speed, the engine would either fail to accelerate to idle speed or might even decelerate because it could not produce sufficient energy to sustain rotation or to accelerate during the initial phase of the starting cycle. The starter must continue to assist the engine considerably above the self-accelerating speed to avoid a hot or hung false start or a combination of both. faqs.question: How should the starter lever be adjusted if the starter motor runs but does not engage the crankshaft gear?

summary.title: Air Turbine Starter System Overview and Maintenance
summary.long_summary:
The air turbine starter (ATS) receives high‑pressure air from a ground cart, the auxiliary power unit (APU), or a cross‑feed from another operating engine. Air is routed through an air‑control valve to the starter, where it drives the turbine rotor. When the rotor reaches cut‑out speed, the turbine switch opens, cutting the electrical signal to the start valve, which then closes and stops the air flow.

The ATS consists of several housings:
• **Turbine housing** – contains the rotor, rotor‑switch actuator, and nozzle that directs inlet air onto the blades. It includes a containment ring that safely dissipates blade fragments in case of overspeed failure.
• **Transmission housing** – holds reduction gears, clutch components, and the drive coupling, and provides an oil reservoir. Maintenance tasks include checking oil level via a sight gauge, inspecting a magnetic chip detector for metal particles, and verifying the absence of leaks. Oil is added through a port sealed by a vent plug with a ball valve; a magnetic drain plug captures ferrous debris. The ATS uses the same turbine oil as the engine, but the oil does not circulate through the engine.
• **Ring‑gear housing** – internal housing that contains the rotor assembly.
• **Switch housing** – houses the turbine switch and its bracket.

Installation and removal are facilitated by a mounting adapter bolted to the engine’s mounting pad and quick‑detach clamps that connect the starter to the adapter and inlet duct. To remove the starter for overhaul, the electrical line is disconnected, clamps are loosened, and the drive coupling is disengaged before withdrawing the unit.

Normal maintenance therefore focuses on oil quantity and cleanliness, magnetic chip detection, and leak checks, ensuring reliable starter operation and safe removal when required.

[Figure 5-24] The shaft of the butterfly valve is connected through a cam arrangement to a servo piston. When the piston is actuated, its motion on the cam causes rotation of the butterfly valve. The slope of the cam track is designed to provide small initial travel and high initial torque when the starter is actuated. The cam track slope also provides more stable action by increasing the opening time of the valve.

The control assembly is mounted on the regulating valve housing and consists of a control housing in which a solenoid is used to stop the action of the control crank in the off position. [Figure 5-24] The control crank links a pilot valve that meters pressure to the servo piston, with the bellows connected by an air line to the pressure-sensing port on the starter.

Turning on the starter switch energizes the regulating valve solenoid. The solenoid retracts and allows the control crank to rotate to the open position. The control crank is rotated by the control rod spring moving the control rod against the closed end of the bellows. Since the regulating valve is closed and downstream pressure is negligible, the bellows can be fully extended by the bellows spring.

summary.title: Operation of Regulating and Shutoff Bleed Valve
summary.long_summary:
Figures 5‑23 and 5‑24 illustrate a regulating and shut‑off bleed valve. The valve housing contains a butterfly‑type valve whose shaft is linked to a servo piston via a cam arrangement. The cam track is shaped to give a small initial travel with high torque, providing a stable opening action. A control assembly mounted on the housing includes a solenoid that locks the control crank in the off position. The control crank connects a pilot valve, which meters air pressure to the servo piston, to a bellows that senses downstream pressure via an air line.

When the starter switch is turned on, the solenoid retracts, freeing the control crank to rotate to the open position. A spring pushes the control rod against the bellows, fully extending it because downstream pressure is initially negligible. As the crank turns, the pilot‑valve rod opens, allowing filtered upstream air to enter the servo‑piston chamber while the drain side closes. The piston moves inward, and the cam converts this linear motion into rotary motion of the butterfly shaft, opening the regulating valve.

Downstream pressure then rises, bleeding back to the bellows and compressing it. This motion drives the control rod, turning the crank further and gradually moving the pilot‑valve rod toward the vent position. When the regulated downstream pressure reaches its preset value, the inflow of air to the servo piston equals the bleed‑to‑atmosphere flow, achieving equilibrium. If both the bleed valve and start valve remain open, regulated air continues to flow through the starter inlet housing.

Many types of turbine starters have included several different methods for turning the engine for starting. Several methods have been used but most of these have given way to electric or air turbine starters. A typical cartridge/pneumatic turbine engine starter may be operated as an ordinary air turbine starter from a ground-operated air supply or an engine cross-bleed source. It may also be operated as a cartridge starter. [Figure 5-15] To accomplish a cartridge start, a cartridge is first placed in the breech cap. The breech is then closed on the breech chamber by means of the breech handle and then rotated a partial turn to engage the lugs between the two breech sections. The cartridge is ignited by applying voltage through the connector at the end of the breech handle. Upon ignition, the cartridge begins to generate gas. The gas is forced out of the breech to the hot gas nozzles that are directed toward the buckets on the turbine rotor, and rotation is produced via the overboard exhaust collector. Before reaching the nozzle, the hot gas passes an outlet leading to the relief valve. This valve directs hot gas to the turbine, bypassing the hot gas nozzle, as the pressure rises above the preset maximum. Thus, the pressure of the gas within the hot gas circuit is maintained at the optimum level.

summary.title: Gas Turbine Engine Starting Methods and Cartridge Starter Operation
summary.long_summary:
Figure 5‑14 illustrates a typical gas‑turbine start sequence, showing compressor RPM and exhaust‑gas temperature versus time. The sequence proceeds as follows: fuel is introduced, ignition is activated, the engine lights up (indicated by a rise in EGT), the engine reaches self‑accelerating speed, the starter disengages, idle RPM is achieved, and the peak starting exhaust‑gas temperature is recorded.

Current gas‑turbine starters fall into three basic categories: direct‑current (DC) electric motors, starter‑generators, and air‑turbine starters. Historically, many different starter concepts were tried, but most have been superseded by electric or air‑turbine systems. One alternative, the air‑impingement starter, directs jets of compressed air onto the compressor or turbine rotor blades to spin the engine; this method is occasionally used on small engines.

A common modern solution is the cartridge/pneumatic starter, which can operate either as a conventional air‑turbine starter using ground‑provided air or an engine cross‑bleed source, or as a cartridge starter. For a cartridge start, a cartridge is placed in the breech cap, the breech is closed, and the handle is rotated to lock the lugs. An electrical pulse ignites the cartridge, producing high‑pressure gas that exits the breech and is channeled through hot‑gas nozzles aimed at the turbine rotor buckets, causing rotation. Before reaching the nozzles, the gas passes a relief valve that diverts excess pressure back to the turbine, maintaining optimal pressure in the hot‑gas circuit.

Figure 5‑15 provides a schematic of this cartridge/pneumatic starter, labeling components such as the cartridge, breech handle and cap, hot‑gas nozzles, relief valve, turbine rotor, compressed‑air inlet, switches, spline shaft, overrunning sprag clutch, gear shaft, and other auxiliary parts. Together, these diagrams and descriptions convey the essential mechanisms by which gas‑turbine engines are started, highlighting the transition from older starter types to the efficient cartridge/pneumatic systems now prevalent in many aircraft and industrial turbines.

The carrying arm transmits torque from the planet gears to the starter jaw as follows:

  1. The cylindrical portion of the carrying arm is splined longitudinally around the inner surface.
  2. Mating splines are cut on the exterior surface of the cylindrical part of the starter jaw.
  3. The jaw slides fore and aft inside the carrying arm to engage and disengage with the engine.

The three planet gears also engage the surrounding internal teeth on the six steel clutch plates. [Figure 5-6] These plates are interleaved with externally splined bronze clutch plates that engage the sides of the housing, preventing them from turning. The proper pressure is maintained upon the clutch pack by a clutch spring retainer assembly. A cylindrical traveling nut inside the starter jaw extends and retracts the jaw. Spiral jaw-engaging splines around the inner wall of the nut mate with similar splines cut on an extension of the sun gear shaft. [Figure 5-6]

Being splined in this fashion, rotation of the shaft forces the nut out and the nut carries the jaw with it. A jaw spring around the traveling nut carries the jaw with the nut and tends to keep a conical clutch surface around the inner wall of the jaw head seated against a similar surface around the underside of the nut head. A return spring is installed on the sun gear shaft extension between a shoulder, formed by the splines around the inner wall of the traveling nut, and a jaw stop retaining nut on the end of the shaft. Because the conical clutch surfaces of the traveling nut and the starter jaw are engaged by jaw spring pressure, the two parts tend to rotate at the same speed. However, the sun gear shaft extension turns six times faster than the jaw. The spiral splines on it are cut left hand, and the sun gear shaft extension, turning to the right in relation to the jaw, forces the traveling nut and the jaw out from the starter its full travel (about 5/16 inches) in approximately 12° of rotation of the jaw.

summary.title: Starter Gear Section and Torque Transmission Mechanism
summary.long_summary:
Figure 5‑6 illustrates a starter gear assembly, focusing on the planetary gear section and its interaction with the starter jaw. The planetary gears are mounted on shafts supported by a barrel‑like planetary carrying arm. Torque from the planet gears is conveyed to the starter jaw through splined connections: the carrying arm’s inner surface carries longitudinal splines, while matching splines are cut on the exterior of the starter jaw’s cylindrical part, allowing the jaw to slide fore and aft for engagement and disengagement with the engine.

Six steel clutch plates, interleaved with externally splined bronze plates, mesh with the planet gears and are held stationary by the housing. A clutch spring retainer maintains proper pressure on this clutch pack. Inside the starter jaw, a cylindrical traveling nut moves axially; spiral splines on its inner wall engage complementary splines on an extension of the sun‑gear shaft. Rotation of the sun‑gear shaft drives the nut outward, pulling the jaw with it. A jaw spring surrounds the traveling nut, keeping a conical clutch surface between the nut head and the jaw head engaged, while a return spring on the sun‑gear shaft extension limits travel.

Because the sun‑gear shaft extension rotates six times faster than the jaw and its left‑hand spiral splines force the nut and jaw outward, the jaw completes its full 5/16‑inch travel in roughly 12° of jaw rotation, completing the starter’s engagement cycle.

The procedures listed in Figure 5-19 are typical of those used to repair malfunctions in a starter generator starting system similar to the system described in this section. These procedures are presented as a guide only. The appropriate manufacturer's instructions and approved maintenance directives should always be consulted for the aircraft involved.

Air Turbine Starters

Air turbine starters are designed to provide high starting torque from a small, lightweight source. The typical air turbine starter weighs from one-fourth to one-half as much as an electric starter capable of starting the same engine. It is capable of developing considerable more torque than the electric starter.

The typical air turbine starter consists of an axial flow turbine that turns a drive coupling through a reduction gear train and a starter clutch mechanism. The air to operate an air turbine starter is supplied from either a ground-operated air cart, the APU, or a cross-bleed start from an engine already operating.

[Figure 5-20] Only one source of around 30–50 pounds per square inch (psi) is used at a time to start the engines. The pressure in the ducts must be high enough to provide for a complete start with a normal limit minimum of about 30 psi. When starting engines with an air turbine starter, always check the duct pressure prior to the start attempt.

Figure 5-21 is a cutaway view of an air turbine starter. The starter is operated by introducing air of sufficient volume and pressure into the starter inlet. The air passes into the starter turbine housing where it is directed against the rotor blades by the nozzle vanes causing the turbine rotor to turn. As the rotor turns, it drives the reduction gear train and clutch arrangement, which includes the rotor pinion, planet gears and carrier, sprag clutch assembly, output shaft assembly, and drive coupling. The sprag clutch assembly engages automatically as soon as the rotor starts to turn but disengages as soon as the drive coupling turns more rapidly than the rotor side. When the starter reaches this overrun speed, the action of the sprag clutch allows the gear train to coast to a halt. faqs.question: What minimum air pressure is required in the ducts to start an engine with an air turbine starter?
faqs.answer: The ducts must have at least about 30 psi, with a typical operating range of 30–50 psi.

faqs.question: What are the possible sources of air for an air turbine starter?
faqs.answer: Air can be supplied from a ground‑operated air cart, the aircraft’s APU, or a cross‑bleed start from an engine that is already running.

faqs.question: How does the sprag clutch in an air turbine starter operate during a start?
faqs.answer: The sprag clutch engages automatically as soon as the turbine rotor starts to turn and disengages when the drive coupling turns faster than the rotor side, allowing the gear train to coast to a halt at over‑run speed.

faqs.question: If the engine does not rotate during a start attempt, what isolation steps should be performed first?
faqs.answer: Check the battery or external power source voltage, verify continuity of the power and ignition switches, confirm the generator control switch position, and with the start circuit energized, measure voltage across the series relay coil, starter relay coil, and at the starter.

faqs.question: What remedy is recommended if no voltage is present across the starter relay coil during the isolation test?
faqs.answer: Replace the starter relay.

faqs.question: What indication suggests that the starter drive shaft may be sheared, and what should be done?
faqs.answer: If the starter rotates but the engine does not, listen for the sound of starter rotation; a rotating starter with no engine movement indicates a sheared drive shaft, and the engine (or its drive shaft assembly) should be replaced.

faqs.question: When the engine starts but does not accelerate to idle, what is the likely cause and the suggested remedy?
faqs.answer: The likely cause is insufficient starter voltage. The remedy is to use a larger‑capacity ground power unit or charge the batteries to provide higher voltage.

faqs.question: How can a defective ignition system be identified according to the troubleshooting procedures?
faqs.answer: Turn on the system and listen for spark‑igniter operation; absence of the expected spark indicates a defective ignition system.

faqs.question: What actions should be taken if the spark igniters are found to be defective?
faqs.answer: Clean or replace the spark igniters, or replace the exciters or leads to the igniters.

faqs.question: Why must duct pressure be checked before attempting to start an engine with an air turbine starter?
faqs.answer: Adequate duct pressure (minimum about 30 psi) is required to supply sufficient air volume and pressure for a complete start; insufficient pressure can prevent the engine from starting.

summary.title: Starter Generator Starting System Troubleshooting Guide
summary.long_summary:
The passage outlines the operation of air‑turbine starters and provides a step‑by‑step troubleshooting matrix for starter‑generator starting systems. Air turbine starters deliver high torque from a lightweight source, weighing only one‑quarter to one‑half of an equivalent electric starter, and generate more torque. They consist of an axial‑flow turbine, reduction gear train, and a clutch mechanism. Air is supplied from a ground cart, the APU, or a cross‑bleed start, typically at 30–50 psi, and only one source is used at a time. Before each start, duct pressure must be verified (minimum ≈30 psi). The turbine’s rotor turns the gear train; a sprag clutch engages automatically and disengages when the drive coupling exceeds rotor speed, allowing the gear train to coast while the engine continues to run.

The troubleshooting table lists three main failure modes:
1. **Engine does not rotate during start attempt** – possible causes include low supply voltage, defective power or ignition switches, faulty relays (start‑lockout, battery series, starter, start‑lock‑in), a defective starter, or a sheared drive shaft. Isolation steps involve checking battery voltage, switch continuity, relay coil voltage, and listening for starter rotation. Remedies range from adjusting voltage, replacing switches, relays, or the starter, to replacing the engine if the drive shaft is damaged.
2. **Engine starts but does not accelerate to idle** – caused by insufficient starter voltage; check terminal voltage and use a higher‑capacity power source or charge batteries.
3. **Engine fails to start when throttle is at idle** – due to a defective ignition system; verify spark‑igniter operation and clean or replace igniters, exciters, or leads.

The guide emphasizes consulting manufacturer instructions and approved maintenance directives for the specific aircraft.

faqs.question: What components are shown in the cutaway view of the air turbine starter in Figure 5‑21?
faqs.answer: Figure 5‑21 shows the internal components of the air turbine starter: the turbine rotor, air inlet, air outlet, engine drive shaft, clutch, and reduction gear.

faqs.question: Which external components are displayed in Figure 5‑22 of the air turbine starter?
faqs.answer: Figure 5‑22 illustrates the external components and connections: the QAD adapter, oil fill plug, QAD coupling clamp, magnetic oil drain plug, sight glass, oil level overflow, and the air inlet and exhaust paths. The forward (FWD) direction is also indicated.

faqs.question: What is the purpose of the pressure‑regulating and shutoff valve in the air turbine starter system?
faqs.answer: The pressure‑regulating and shutoff valve (also called the bleed valve) controls the duct pressure flowing to the starter inlet ducting, regulates the pressure of the starter operating air, and shuts off the air supply to the engine when the valve is selected off.

faqs.question: How does air reach the starter after passing through the pressure‑regulating and shutoff valve?
faqs.answer: After the pressure‑regulating and shutoff valve, the air flows downstream to the start valve, which controls the airflow into the starter.

faqs.question: What are the two sub‑assemblies that make up the pressure‑regulating and shutoff valve?
faqs.answer: The pressure‑regulating and shutoff valve consists of two sub‑assemblies: the pressure‑regulating valve and the pressure‑shutoff valve.

faqs.question: In Figure 5‑22, where does the air enter and exit the air turbine starter?
faqs.answer: Air enters the starter through the air inlet and exits through the exhaust (air outlet) as shown in Figure 5‑22.

faqs.question: What indicates the forward direction on the air turbine starter diagram?
faqs.answer: The forward (FWD) direction is indicated on the diagram in Figure 5‑22.

faqs.question: What is the function of the sight glass shown in Figure 5‑22?
faqs.answer: The sight glass, shown in Figure 5‑22, is used to view the oil level within the starter.

summary.title: Air Turbine Starter Components and Air‑Flow Control
summary.long_summary:
Figures 5‑21 and 5‑22 illustrate an air turbine starter. Figure 5‑21 is a cutaway view showing internal parts such as the turbine rotor, air inlet and outlet, engine‑drive shaft, clutch, and reduction gear; air enters the rotor, spins it, and the reduction gear and clutch transmit torque to the engine. Figure 5‑22 presents the external layout, labeling the QAD adapter, oil‑fill plug, QAD coupling clamp, magnetic oil‑drain plug, sight glass, and oil‑level overflow. The diagram also indicates the forward (FWD) direction of rotation and the path of air entering through the inlet and exiting as exhaust.

The accompanying text explains the air‑flow path to the starter. Air is first routed through a combined pressure‑regulating and shut‑off (bleed) valve, which sets the duct pressure supplied to the starter inlet and can cut off the air supply when the starter is turned off. Downstream of this bleed valve, a separate start valve governs the actual flow of air into the starter. The pressure‑regulating and shut‑off valve is composed of two sub‑assemblies: a pressure‑regulating valve and a pressure‑shut‑off valve, which together maintain proper operating pressure and provide safety shut‑off capability.
